food.text: Native American peoples lived off the land across very diverse bioregions, often leading a nomadic life in which their diet changed with the seasons. Before 1600 they had done so for thousands of years. Nearly all regions of present-day American cuisine have roots in these foodways.

The most important Indigenous American crops have generally included Indian corn, beans, squash, pumpkins, sunflowers, wild rice, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, peanuts, avocados, potatoes and chocolate. The word maize comes from the Taíno name for the plant.

European colonists introduced sugar, flour, milk, eggs and livestock to the North American colonies. Enslaved West Africans, trafficked to the colonies through the Atlantic slave trade, introduced black-eyed peas, okra, eggplant, sesame, sorghum, melons and various spices.
food.source_title: Cuisine of the Southern United States

food.text: In the 17th century, French colonists settled Acadia and adapted their 16th-century French cuisine to the crops, seafood and animals that flourished there. Their descendants became the Acadian people. Vegetables such as potato, onion, carrot, turnip, beet, squash and corn were popular because they kept well in root cellars and jars for the winter.

Southeastern Native Americans gave the Southern diet one of its main staples: corn, either ground into meal or limed with an alkaline salt to make hominy. This Native American technique is known as nixtamalization. Corn also became familiar cornbread and grits.

The Apalachee of Florida hunted deer, rabbit, raccoon and turkey. They grew corn, beans, squash and sunflowers in their gardens and foraged for wild berries and nuts. They influenced Spanish colonists, who enjoyed Native American cacina tea and turkey.
food.source_title: Cuisine of the Southern United States

food.text: After the British established a permanent settlement at Jamestown in 1607, ham from Britain evolved into Virginia hams, and English breads became hot breads and other sweets. The predominant cooks in Virginia's kitchens were enslaved African Americans. Enslaved cooks in white plantation homes combined food traditions from West Africa with Native American and European cooking methods, creating new dishes such as fried okra.
food.source_title: Cuisine of the Southern United States

food.text: The influx of United Empire Loyalists into British North America in the 18th century brought British cooking to the future province of Ontario. Early English-Canadians in Upper Canada added wild berries, maple sugar, venison, partridge, waterfowl, maize, pumpkin and turkey to their meals. Early meals relied heavily on pork and potatoes, and roasting was a common method of cooking.

Rice became prominent in many dishes in the Lowcountry region of South Carolina because the enslaved people who settled the region, now known as the Gullah people, were already familiar with the crop. Planters in the Carolinas and Georgia discovered that African rice would grow there and often sought out enslaved Africans from rice-growing regions, because they had the skills and knowledge to build irrigation, dams and earthworks.
food.source_title: Cuisine of the Southern United States

food.text: Some Sephardic Jews fled the Inquisition in the 15th century and settled in Recife, Brazil and the West Indies. There, new local ingredients such as molasses, rum, sugar, vanilla, chocolate, peppers, corn, tomatoes, kidney beans, string beans and turkey shaped their cuisine. In 1654, 23 Sephardic Jews arrived in New Amsterdam, bringing this cuisine to the early colonial United States, where it heavily influenced early American Jewish cuisine.

After the English conquered Acadia in the 18th century, they decided to deport the Acadians and take their settlements, which were often built on the most fertile earth in the colony. Most Acadians did not manage to escape the deportation. Of those who did, most fled to the east and north of New Brunswick, so Acadian cuisine was refocused around what could be grown, hunted and fished in the less fertile lands of the East Coast of New Brunswick and the Upper St. John River Valley.

The Maliseet, Mi'kmaq and Penobscot peoples introduced the fiddlehead fern to the Acadians in the early 18th century. It remains a popular Acadian dish. Maple sugar is also a popular sweetener, given the ties between Quebec and Acadia.

art.text: St. Augustine, Florida, founded in 1565, is the first continuously European-occupied city in North America. Beginning in 1598, coquina quarried on Anastasia Island shaped a new colonial style of architecture there. Coquina is a limestone conglomerate containing small mollusk shells.

When Francisco Vásquez de Coronado crossed the Southwest in search of mythical cities of gold, he found the ancient culture and architecture of the Pueblo people instead. Pueblo dwellings were built of adobe, a sun-dried clay brick, with exposed wooden ceiling beams. Their cubic form and dense arrangement gave the villages a singular look.

Coquina, a limestone full of tiny mollusk shells, was used to build St. Augustine's homes, its City Gate and its Cathedral Basilica. It also went into the Castillo de San Marcos and Fort Matanzas. Today the city is one of the rare vestiges of 17th-century Spanish colonial architecture in the United States.

The Spanish conquered the Pueblo villages and in 1609 made Pueblo de Santa Fe the administrative capital of the Santa Fe de Nuevo México Province. The Palace of the Governors was built there between 1610 and 1614 as a long building with a patio, mixing Pueblo Indian and Spanish influences.

In Boston and Salem in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, the Georgian style took hold, but in a simpler form than in England, adapted to colonial limitations. Religious buildings of the period, such as Saint Paul's Chapel (1766) in New York, typically featured brick, stone-like stucco and a single spire above the entrance.

Indigenous art of the Americas has been collected by Europeans since sustained contact in 1492. The first cabinets of curiosities in the 16th century, precursors to modern museums, featured Native American art.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

art.text: The Mission San Francisco de Asis in Ranchos de Taos, New Mexico, dates from the 1770s and used the adobe technique. This gave the building a striking look of bold austerity. Centuries later, the Pueblo Revival Style developed in the region.

The Mission San Xavier del Bac near Tucson, Arizona, has Churrigueresque detailing drawn from southern examples in New Spain. Its facade is framed by two massive towers, and the entrance is flanked by estipites.

Architect Peter Harrison used European techniques to design the Redwood Library and Athenaeum in Newport, Rhode Island, in 1748 and 1761. It is now the oldest community library still occupying its original building in the United States.

Some Indigenous art forms coincide with Western ones, but others, such as porcupine quillwork and birchbark biting, are unique to the Americas. Portable Indigenous arts include painting, basketry and textiles, while monumental works include architecture, land art and murals.
art.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

war.text: The American Revolutionary War lasted from April 19, 1775 to September 3, 1783. American Patriot forces organized as the Continental Army and commanded by George Washington defeated the British Army. In the 1783 Treaty of Paris, the British monarchy acknowledged the independence of the Thirteen Colonies.

In the Northwest Indian War, a pan-tribal confederacy led by Blue Jacket, Little Turtle, Buckongahelas and Egushawa defeated armies led by Generals Josiah Harmar and Arthur St. Clair. St. Clair's defeat was the most severe loss ever inflicted upon an American army by Indians.

The Beaver Wars were conflicts fought intermittently during the 17th century around the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River valley. The Haudenosaunee, supported by the Dutch and later the English, fought the Wendat, who were supported by the French. One theory says the Haudenosaunee needed to replenish their population after catastrophic epidemics such as smallpox in the 1630s. When a family member died, a raid was often needed to capture a replacement from an enemy group, who was adopted and took the dead person's name and role. Larger raids meant more deaths, which in turn required more captives. Some scholars call the brutal warfare genocide, while others disagree.

The outcome of the Revolutionary War seemed uncertain for most of the conflict. Washington and the Continental Army's decisive victory in the Siege of Yorktown in 1781 led King George III and Great Britain to negotiate an end to the war.

The Battles of Lexington and Concord in April 1775 were the first battles of the Revolutionary War. In June 1775, the Second Continental Congress voted to fold colonial Patriot militias into a central Continental Army. It unanimously appointed Washington as its commander-in-chief.

The Battle of Fallen Timbers was fought on 20 August 1794 among trees toppled by a tornado near the Maumee River in northwestern Ohio. Anthony Wayne's Legion of the United States, supported by Kentucky militia, defeated a combined Native American force, with fighting that turned to hand-to-hand combat, grapeshot blasted into the Native American line, and a bayonet charge. Wayne's army lost 33 men and had about 100 wounded; Egushawa was shot through the eye, and Turkey Foot was shot in the chest and died almost instantly. The battle lasted little more than one hour, and the survivors fled to Fort Miami, only to find its gates closed against them.

The capture of Pocahontas by Captain Samuel Argall in 1613 made Powhatan sue for peace during the First Anglo-Powhatan War. Peace came with her marriage to the tobacco planter John Rolfe on April 5, 1614. Earlier in the war, the colonists had effectively destroyed two subtribes, the Kecoughtan and the Paspahegh.

Queen Anne's War, from 1702 to 1713, was the North American theater of the War of the Spanish Succession. English frontier settlements and areas around Charleston, South Carolina were raided by the French and their Native American allies. In the 1710 Siege of Port Royal, Britain conquered Acadia, which became the province of Nova Scotia.

Defeat at Saratoga in 1777 made it clear to Britain that the revolt would not be easily suppressed, especially after the Franco-American alliance of February 1778. With Spain also expected to join, the Royal Navy had to prioritize either America or Europe. Lord George Germain favored America, while the Earl of Sandwich favored Europe.

After Fallen Timbers, the native nations realized that British assistance was not forthcoming. They were compelled to sign the Treaty of Greenville in 1795, which ceded Ohio and part of Indiana to the United States.

In June 1687, Governor Denonville set out with a well organized force to Fort Frontenac and captured 58 male prisoners. Thirty-six of them were later shipped to Marseille, France to be galley slaves, and only 13 survived to return to Canada. The Iroquois retaliated by destroying farmsteads and slaughtering entire families. They burned Lachine to the ground on August 4, 1689.

In May 1791, Lieutenant Colonel James Wilkinson raided Kenapacomaqua, killing nine Wea and Miami and capturing 34 Miami as prisoners, including a daughter of Little Turtle. Wilkinson thought the raid was clever. Many confederation leaders had been weighing peace terms, but when they heard of it they readied for war. The raid had the opposite effect from the one intended, uniting the tribes against St. Clair.

literature.text: Phillis Wheatley was an enslaved African woman who became the first African American to publish a book of poetry. Her collection, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, appeared in 1773, three years before American independence.
tags: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral

literature.text: The population of the British colonies grew from approximately 111,000 in 1670 to more than 250,000 thirty years later. By 1760 it reached 1,600,000. This growth brought a greater diversity of opinion in religious and political life, which showed in the literature of the time.

In 1789 Olaudah Equiano published The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, an autobiography. It became one of the first influential works about the transatlantic slave trade and the experiences of enslaved Africans. It appeared sixteen years after Phillis Wheatley's book.

Phillis Wheatley was born in Senegal or The Gambia and was captured and sold into slavery at around the age of seven. She was kidnapped to Massachusetts, where a Boston merchant purchased her and owned her. By the time she was 16 she had mastered English, and she went on to become the first African American to publish a book of poetry.

Born in Senegal or The Gambia, Wheatley was captured and sold into slavery at around the age of seven. She was kidnapped to Massachusetts, where a Boston merchant purchased her and owned her. By the time she was 16, she had mastered English. George Washington thanked her for a poem written in his honor.

Jupiter Hammon, a domestic slave in Queens, New York, is considered the first published Black writer in America. He published his poem "An Evening Thought: Salvation by Christ with Penitential Cries" as a broadside in early 1761.

Mather's The Christian Philosopher (1721) was the first book published in North America that promoted Newton and natural theology. It reflected a shift in 18th-century writing from the Puritanism of Winthrop and Bradford toward reason in the Age of Enlightenment.

William Hill Brown's The Power of Sympathy, published in 1791 (the article elsewhere gives 1789), is described as an early American novel. It depicts a tragic love story between siblings who fell in love without knowing they were related. The period around the American Revolution is also notable for the political writings of Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Paine, and Thomas Jefferson.

Phillis Wheatley published Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral in 1773, three years before American independence. She was not only the first African American to publish a book but also the first to achieve an international reputation as a writer.
tags: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral

literature.text: In 1778 Jupiter Hammon wrote an ode to Phillis Wheatley. In it he discussed their shared humanity and common bonds.

Cadwallader Colden's The History of the Five Indian Nations, published in 1727, was one of the first texts published on Iroquois history. Colden also wrote a book on botany that attracted the attention of Carl Linnaeus, and he kept up a long correspondence with Benjamin Franklin.
tags: The History of the Five Indian Nations

literature.text: Growing communities and social life made colonists more interested in the progress of individuals and their shared experience. These new ideas can be seen in the popularity of Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography.
Phillis Wheatley's poetry was praised by leading figures of the American Revolution. George Washington thanked her for a poem she had written in his honor.
tags: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral

science.text: In 1721, Boston suffered its worst smallpox outbreak: 5,759 of around 10,600 people were infected and 844 were recorded to have died between April 1721 and February 1722. At its peak in October, 411 people died in that month alone, and 8% of Boston's population would die during the epidemic. Hundreds of other Bostonians recovered with severe scarring or disabilities. The outbreak led Cotton Mather and physician Zabdiel Boylston to variolate hundreds of Bostonians in the Thirteen Colonies' earliest experiment with public inoculation.

The American Philosophical Society was founded in Philadelphia in 1743 by Benjamin Franklin and others. It is considered the first learned society founded in what became the United States, and it promotes knowledge in the humanities and natural sciences.

John Winthrop the Younger, an early governor of the Connecticut Colony, was an avid scientist who experimented on obtaining salt from sea water. In 1663 he was elected an original fellow of the Royal Society while visiting England.

Benjamin Banneker, the son of a free African-American mother and a formerly enslaved father, had little or no formal education and was largely self-taught. His knowledge of astronomy helped him author a commercially successful series of almanacs.

On 26 June 1721, Zabdiel Boylston first inoculated his six-year-old son Thomas, then his 36-year-old slave and the slave's two-year-old son, using a method that deliberately gave them smallpox. All three survived relatively mild cases without disability or disfigurement. Over five months he inoculated 247 people in and around Boston, and 6 of them died.

David Rittenhouse's 1763-1764 survey of the Delaware-Pennsylvania border was a 12-mile circle about the Court House in New Castle, Delaware. His work was so precise and well documented that it was incorporated without modification into Mason and Dixon's survey of the Pennsylvania-Maryland border.

Boylston's 247 inoculated patients had a 2% death rate, versus the 15% of people who died if they got smallpox naturally. Even so, variolation carried a real risk of death, and Boylston was ridiculed in the newspapers as a quack, assaulted in the streets, and threatened so badly that he hid in his house for two weeks. In 1723 he traveled to England and received honors by King George, and in London he published An Historical Account of the Smallpox Inoculated in New England.
tags: An Historical Account of the Smallpox Inoculated in New England

science.text: In 1786, the American Philosophical Society established the Magellanic Premium, a prize for achievement in "navigation, astronomy, or natural philosophy." It is the oldest scientific prize awarded by an American institution, and the society still awards it.

During his 1661 to 1663 trip to England, John Winthrop the Younger showed New World plants and animals to Charles II. The King was particularly interested in milkweed and wanted a pillow made from it, until he was convinced that it was impractical.

Banneker's surviving journal, described in April 1800, recalled the 1749, 1766 and 1783 emergences of Brood X of the seventeen-year periodical cicada. It also described an effect that the pathogenic fungus Massospora cicadina has on its host, and recorded his observations on the hives and behavior of honey bees. On the day of Banneker's funeral, a fire destroyed all but one of his journals, so this is the only one that survived.

The first coins struck at the United States Mint were made from flatware provided by George Washington on the morning of July 30, 1792. David Rittenhouse, the Mint's first director, hand-struck them to test the new equipment and gave them to Washington as a token of appreciation.

politics.text: The first permanent English colony in the Americas was established at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607. The colonists faced extreme adversity: by 1617 only 351 of the 1700 colonists transported to Jamestown were still alive. The colony grew into the Colony of Virginia, and the Crown took direct control of the venture in 1624, after the London Company went bankrupt in part because of frequent warring with nearby American Indians.

The Treaty of Paris of 1763 formally ended the Seven Years' War, called the French and Indian War by the English colonies. Britain acquired most of New France, more than doubling its territory in North America and dramatically changing the continent's political landscape.
The 1713 Treaty of Utrecht ended the War of Spanish Succession. Britain won the French territories of Newfoundland and Acadia, and Acadia was renamed Nova Scotia.
England annexed the Dutch colony of New Netherland in 1664, following the capture of New Amsterdam. The city was renamed New York.

Puritan separatists later known as the Pilgrims founded Plymouth in 1620. Fleeing religious persecution became a major motive for English colonists, and Maryland was founded by English Roman Catholics in 1634 while Rhode Island in 1636 was tolerant of all religions.

In the 1730s, James Oglethorpe proposed colonizing the area south of the Carolinas as a buffer against Spanish Florida. He and his fellow trustees hoped for a utopian colony that banned slavery, but Georgia was sparsely populated by 1750 and became a crown colony in 1752.

In 1786, Thomas Jefferson asserted that the United States must be viewed as the nest from which all America, North and South, is to be peopled. He added that "The navigation of the Mississippi we must have".

The 1786–1795 Northwest Indian War saw the United States fight the Northwestern Confederacy over land around the Great Lakes. Treaties such as Greenville and Fort Wayne fueled anti-American sentiment among Native Americans, leading to Tecumseh's Confederacy.
During the War of Jenkins' Ear, which merged with King George's War in North America in 1742, Spanish privateers attacked the coast of North Carolina. They levied tribute on the inhabitants there.

philosophy.text: Early American philosophy in the 17th and 18th centuries is largely seen as an extension of the European Enlightenment. Colonial America was influenced by the Puritan thought of Samuel Johnson and Jonathan Edwards. The Enlightenment also shaped the philosophy of the American Revolution and Founding Fathers such as Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson.

Beginning in the 1600s, European Christians, both Catholics and various Protestants, sought to convert Native American tribes from their existing beliefs to Christianity. After the United States gained independence in the late 1700s, its government continued to suppress Indigenous practices and promote forcible conversion, often working together with religious organizations. In many cases violence was used as a tool of suppression, as in the government's violent eradication of Ghost Dance and Sun Dance practitioners in the 1890s.

Benjamin Franklin was considered America's first philosopher, at a time when the word also covered natural philosophy and the broad application of reason to well-being. He founded the Junto in 1727 and the American Philosophical Society in 1743.

Anne Hutchinson was influenced by the minister John Cotton and took part in the Antinomian Controversy, which disrupted Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1636 to 1638. She was put on trial for preferring a covenant of grace to a covenant of works.

Yale University was founded in Connecticut in 1701 by a group of Harvard alumni who were also Congregationalist clergymen. Two of its brilliant students, Samuel Johnson and Jonathan Edwards, developed their own American theology and philosophy as modern philosophy and the Enlightenment reached colonial America.

The Longhouse Religion, or Code of Handsome Lake, was founded in 1797 or 1799 by the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake. It reinterpreted traditional Seneca beliefs with a code that forbade drinking, selling of land and witchcraft, aiming to revive traditional consciousness after a long period of cultural disintegration following colonization.

Central to Lakota religion is wakʽą, an energy or power permeating the universe. Lakota religionists believe that, because they share wakʽą, humans exist in kinship with all life forms, a relationship that informs their behavior.

Midewiwin, or the Grand Medicine Society, is a religious society of Indigenous peoples of the Maritimes, New England, and Great Lakes regions. Its societies keep wiigwaasabak, birch bark scrolls that preserve their teachings, and have degrees of initiation.
After her trial, Anne Hutchinson fled with supporters such as John Clarke and William Coddington. With encouragement from Roger Williams, they established Portsmouth, Rhode Island.

Benjamin Franklin's American Philosophical Society, founded in 1743, drew in associates such as botanist John Bartram and silversmith Philip Syng. Syng made the inkstand later used to sign the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Newton critic Cadwallader Colden joined a year later.

In the British Thirteen Colonies, James Bowdoin, John Adams and John Hancock founded the American Academy of Arts and Sciences at Boston during the American War of Independence. Benjamin Franklin had founded the American Philosophical Society in 1743.
tags: American Academy of Arts and Sciences

philosophy.text: The Seven Fires prophecy was originally taught among practitioners of Midewiwin. Each fire represents a prophetical age of Turtle Island, and the prophecy suggests that the different colors and traditions of humans can come together on the basis of respect.

Christian contact with the Sioux-speaking peoples began around 1665, when the Jesuit missionaries Claude Allouez and Jacques Marquette met with Dakota groups. Missionaries later tried to adapt traditional beliefs, using the term Wakʽą Tʽąką to describe their God and wakʽą šicų for demons.

culture.text: After Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage, plants, animals, culture, people, technology and ideas moved between the Americas and the Old World in what is called the Columbian exchange. For Native American cultures the effect was generally destructive, through disease and a clash of cultures: European values of private property, smaller family structures and labor led to conflict, the appropriation of traditional communal lands and slavery.
culture.source_title: Native American cultures in the United States

culture.text: Up to the early to mid 18th century, the term Americans was not applied to people of European heritage in North America. Instead it meant the same as the term Indians. Only later did people of European heritage begin using Americans to refer to themselves.
culture.source_title: Native Americans in the United States

culture.text: The Spanish language first arrived in present-day New Mexico with Juan de Oñate's colonization expedition in 1598, which brought 600-700 settlers. Almost half the early settlers were from Spain, while most of the rest came from various parts of Latin America, the Canary Islands, and Portugal.

In 1775 Daniel Boone blazed a trail for the Transylvania Company from Virginia through the Cumberland Gap into central Kentucky. The Wilderness Road was steep and rough and could only be traversed on foot or horseback, but it was the best route for thousands of settlers. Settlers on it faced Native attacks: in 1784 alone, Natives killed over 100 travelers on the Wilderness Road, and Abraham Lincoln's grandfather was scalped near Louisville that year after a raiding party intercepted him.

By the start of the 16th century, Sioux-speaking peoples lived on the headwaters of the River Mississippi; by the time they first met Europeans in the mid-17th century, they belonged to a confederation called the Oceti Šakowin, or Seven Council Fires. From 1640 Europeans called them the Sioux, a term borrowed from the Ojibwe, in whose language it was a pejorative word meaning 'lesser, or small, adder.'

Following the Pueblo Revolt in 1680, New Mexico was resettled again, starting in 1692, primarily by refugees from the revolt and others born in northern New Spain. A dialect of Spanish has been spoken there uninterruptedly since the end of the seventeenth century.

In the American Southwest, especially New Mexico, Catholicism brought by Spanish missionaries blended with Indigenous religions. The religious drums, chants and dances of the Pueblo people are regularly part of Masses at Santa Fe's Saint Francis Cathedral.
culture.source_title: Native American cultures in the United States

culture.text: By 1750 the Native American slave trade had effectively ended, after devastating wars among the tribes such as the Yamasee War. Surviving peoples of the southeast strengthened loose coalitions of language groups and joined confederacies such as the Choctaw, the Creek and the Catawba for protection.
culture.source_title: Native Americans in the United States

culture.text: Christian contact with Sioux-speaking peoples began circa 1665, when the Jesuit missionaries Claude Allouez and Jacques Marquette met with Dakota groups. Sporadic Roman Catholic missionary visits followed throughout the 17th and 18th centuries.
In the 18th century the Lakota were among the Sioux-speaking peoples who began to migrate west, encouraged by conflict with the Ojibwe and Cree. After 1750 they entered the Black Hills area.
